title.en: The Sword-Fish and the Plantain Rampart: Hang Nadim's Idea
title.zh: 劍魚與芭蕉堤：漢·納丁之策

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. X (the todak sword-fish), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: The sword-fish todak come upon the coast of Singhapura, springing ashore to pierce men through and through, until none dare live on the beach. Paduka Sri Maharaja marches out and orders a rampart of his men's legs — until a boy among the people says: 'Of what use is a rampart of our legs? It would be much better to make a rampart of plantain stems.' The beaks bury themselves in the banana trunks and the fish are slain in heaps; and the great men, awed by the boy's understanding, counsel the raja to kill him before he grows — 'and he was accordingly put to death, but the guilt of his blood' remains in the chronicle's telling.
summary.zh: 劍魚（todak）湧至獅子城海岸，躍上岸穿透人體，海灘無人敢居。帕杜卡·斯里·摩訶拉賈親征，命部下以腿築壘——人群中一男孩言：『以腿築壘何用？不如以芭蕉莖為堤。』魚喙盡沒入蕉莖，劍魚成堆被殺；而大臣們懼此童之才，勸王於其長成前除之——『於是殺之，然其血之罪』永載紀年。

sensitivity.note: The Hang Nadim episode; the killing of the clever child is the chronicle's own commentary on royal fear.

passages.text: A species of sword-fish named todak came upon the coast of Singhapura, and springing ashore killed a great number of persons on the beach — striking the breast they pierced through the body to the back; so many were slain that nobody durst reside on the shore.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. X (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Paduka Sri Maharaja marched out with all his ministers and warriors, and ordered a rampart to be formed of the legs of his men; but the sword-fish sprung out and pierced their limbs through and through. Among the people there was a boy who said: 'Of what use is it for us to form a rampart with our legs? It would be much better to make a rampart of plantain stems.' The raja heard and assented; the sword-fish rapidly struck their beaks into the plantain stems, and remaining there the people came and slew them in great numbers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. X (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: All the great men represented to him: 'Sire, if this boy, though so young, possesses such an uncommon understanding, what will he do when he grows up? It will be best for us to kill him.' He was accordingly put to death, but the guilt of his blood stays with the tellers — the chronicle's verdict on the fear of clever children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. X (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Albicore That Carried Him Ashore: The Taboo of the Alu-alu Fish
title.zh: 載他登岸的鰹魚：禁食鰹魚之禁忌

region.en: Jambu Ayer roadstead, Malay Annals geography
region.zh: 占布·阿耶爾泊地（《馬來紀年》地理）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. XI (Mani Farendan's shipwreck), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Prince Mani Farendan sails for Malacca with a fleet; at Jambu Ayer a violent storm sinks his ship, and fallen into the sea he leaps upon an albicore — the alu-alu fish — by which he is conveyed to land, catching hold of a ganda-suli tree to reach the shore. 'This is the reason that Mani Farendan forbade all his descendants to eat of the fish alu-alu, or to wear the flower of the ganda-suli' — the house's thanksgiving fixed as a food and flower taboo.
summary.zh: 瑪尼·法倫丹王子率船隊往滿剌加；至占布·阿耶爾，暴風驟起沉其船。他墜海中，躍上鰹魚（alu-alu）之背，被載至岸邊，攀住格達-蘇利樹而登陸。『故瑪尼·法倫丹禁其子孫食鰹魚、佩格達-蘇利之花』——家族之感恩定為食禁與花禁。

sensitivity.note: Fish-rescue etiology fixing a family taboo.

passages.text: When Mani Farendan arrived at Jambu Ayer, the wind arose, and a violent storm succeeded, and the ship of Mani Farendan sunk; and he having fallen into the sea leapt upon an albicore, or alu-alu fish, by which he was conveyed to land.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: When he reached the shore he caught hold of a ganda-suli tree, and in this manner reached the land. This is the reason that Mani Farendan forbade all his descendants to eat of the fish alu-alu, or to wear the flower of the ganda-suli — the rescuers of the prince made forever untouchable by his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XI (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fisher-King: Raja Kasim Selling Fish to the Stranger Ship
title.zh: 漁夫王：向異船賣魚的卡西姆王子

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. XIII (Raja Kasim in disguise), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Dispossessed by his father's widow's party, Raja Kasim lives unregarded in the house of a fisherman and plies the fisher's trade at sea. When a vessel from the regions above the wind anchors, all the fishing prows come out to sell fish — among them Raja Kasim; and the merchant Moulana Jelal-ed-din, seeing him, calls him aboard and treats him with all the dignity of his rank. 'Why do you pay respect to me, a poor fisherman?' — 'Of a truth, you are the son of this country, and will certainly become raja of Malaca.'
summary.zh: 被庶母一黨剝奪繼承的卡西姆王子，匿身漁夫之家，操舟賣魚。一艘上風之邦的商船來泊，漁船盡出賣魚——卡西姆亦在其中；船上商人毛拉納·哲拉魯丁見之，請他登船、以王者之禮相待。『緣何禮遇賣魚之窮漁夫？』——『足下實為此國之子，必將為滿剌加之王。』

sensitivity.note: Disguised-king recognition episode; the blessing of the stranger merchant.

passages.text: Raja Kasim went unregarded and lived in the house of a fisherman, and for a long period plied the trade of a fisher at sea. When a vessel from the regions above the wind drew near the land, all the fishing prows and boats approached to sell fish to the people of the vessel; among the rest came Raja Kasim to sell his fish, in the dress of a fisherman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: The merchant Moulana Jelal-ed-din, as soon as he saw Raja Kasim, called him on board and treated him with all the dignity due to his rank. 'Why do you pay respect to me, a poor fisherman selling my fish?' — 'Of a truth, you are the son of this country, and will certainly become raja of Malaca' — the stranger's blessing that begins the restored reign.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. XIII (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pursuit of Dewa Sura: Numbers, Names and the Mound of 'Gently, Gently'
title.zh: 追捕德瓦·蘇拉：數、名與『慢慢來』之丘

region.zh: 賈拉姆-誇伊丘（《馬來紀年》地理）

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals (the pursuit of Maha Raja Dewa Sura), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: Ordered to pursue the fugitive Maha Raja Dewa Sura, the champion Sri Vija di Raja amuses himself — snaring apes, fishing with nets — while everyone else races for the reward. 'How do you youngsters know?' he answers: 'On trying his name by the power of numbers, it is subservient, and his time is also subservient to mine; how then can he escape from my hands?' The fugitive's boat grounds at a mound he names with a cry — kwoi! kwoi! 'gently, gently' in Siamese — the mound keeps the name Jaram-kwoi, and the fugitive is taken at the old woman's hut, without fetters, 'according to the custom of Princes.'
summary.zh: 奉命追捕逃亡的德瓦·蘇拉，勇士斯里·維賈·迪·拉賈卻自得其樂——捕猿、撒網——而人人爭先逐賞。『你們少年人懂什麼？』他答：『以數之力驗其名，其名已服；其時亦服於我時——他豈能逃出我手？』逃者之舟擱於一丘，他以暹語呼『誇伊！誇伊！』（慢慢來）而名之曰賈拉姆-誇伊；逃者在老嫗之屋被擒，不加縛鎖——『依王子之禮相待』。

sensitivity.note: Name-numerology (ilmu) applied to pursuit; the mound-etiology inside the episode.

passages.text: Sri Vija di Raja went on the pursuit, but he amused himself with catching the wild buffalo, piercing the rhinoceros, and snaring the ape, and wherever the sand of the river was fine, there he amused himself in fishing with nets. 'How do you youngsters know?' he said; 'on trying his name by the power of numbers, it is subservient, and his time is also subservient to mine; how then can he escape from my hands?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Malay Annals pursuit episode (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.

passages.text: Maha Raja Deva Sura's boat grounded at the foot of a mound at the mouth of a small river, when he exclaimed 'kwoi! kwoi!' — 'gently, gently' in Siamese; hence the name of the mound is still Jaram-kwoi. There the Malaca men came up with him, and he was taken at the old woman's house and delivered up to the bandahara without fetters or bonds, treated according to the custom of Princes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Malay Annals pursuit episode; not verbatim.

title.en: The First Damasked Krises of Majapahit
title.zh: 馬卓帕希特首批大馬士革紋克利斯

texts.period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the krises of Majapahit

summary.en: In the chronicle's account of the Majapahit period, the smiths' art reaches its highest perfection: 'the first damasked krises were now made by the pandi (smiths) from Pajajaran, who became so distinguished that they were appointed to the charge of districts with a thousand chaka each.' The kris afterwards placed on the tomb of Sunan Giri is said to have been manufactured at this time from a piece of old iron found by the prince — the weapon of state carried from found iron to holy tomb.
summary.zh: 編年史述馬卓帕希特之世，匠藝臻於極盛：『首批大馬士革紋克利斯由帕查查蘭來之鐵匠（pandi）鍛成，彼等名聲大著，各獲授千戶（chaka）之地之職。』後供於蘇南·吉里墓上之克利斯，據云即此時以王子所拾之一塊廢鐵鍛成——武器由拾得之鐵至聖墓完成旅程。

sensitivity.note: Smithing charter of the pusaka-kris tradition.

passages.text: The first damasked krises were now made by the pandi, or smiths, from Pajajaran, who became so distinguished that they were appointed to the charge of districts with a thousand chaka each — the smiths raised to lords of land by their art.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: The kris which was afterwards placed on the tomb of Sunan Giri is said to have been manufactured at this time from a piece of old iron found by the prince — found iron hammered into the holiest of blades.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.

title.en: The Prince in Commoner's Dress: The Arrow of Jaya Langkara's Iron
title.zh: 布衣王子：耶亞·蘭卡拉之鐵箭

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the death of Ino Kerta Pati

summary.en: Finding the battle going against him, the prince of Nusa Antara remembers the guru's advice, the loss of his wife, and the insults of Ino Kerta Pati; throwing off his princely attire he disguises himself as a common man, arms himself with an arrow made from the iron of Jaya Langkara, and goes in search of his enemy — who falls dead at the first shot, 'it having been foretold that this chief could not be killed except by the iron staff of Jaya Langkara, of which the prince of Nusa Antara had made his arrow.'
summary.zh: 戰局逆轉之際，努薩·安塔拉王子想起上師之訓、亡妻之痛與伊諾·克爾塔·巴迪之辱；褪去王服、扮作常人，以耶亞·蘭卡拉之鐵所製之箭為兵器，尋仇而去——一箭而斃，『蓋預言曾云：此人唯耶亞·蘭卡拉之鐵杖能殺，而努薩·安塔拉王子之箭正是以此鐵所製』。

passages.text: This prince, finding the battle going against him, recollected the advice of Guru Bramana Kdenda, the loss of his wife, and the many insults he had received from Ino Karta Pati; then throwing off his princely attire he disguised himself as a common man, and arming himself with an arrow mixed with the poison of Jaraga went in search of Ino Kerta Pati.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: He had no sooner found him than he discharged his arrow, and Ino Kerta Pati fell dead — it having been foretold that this chief could not be killed except by the iron staff of Jaya Langkara, of which the prince of Nusa Antara had made his arrow, arm and knife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.

title.en: The Mountain That Thunders: Plague, Ash-Darkness and the Flight to Sea
title.zh: 轟鳴之山：瘟疫、灰暗與出海之逃

region.en: Mount Kelud, East Java, and the western coast
region.zh: 東爪哇克盧特山與西岸

texts.period: Javanese chronicle tradition recorded by Raffles (1817)

source.work: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1817), vol. II, ch. X, the sickness and eruption of Kelud

summary.en: A dreadful sickness prevails in the eastern districts of Java, and the young prince quits his capital to found a new one in the west — while the first recorded eruption of Mount Kelud discharges 'like thunder,' its ashes involving the country 'in impenetrable darkness.' The sickness continuing after the prince's departure, the inhabitants who remained 'embarked in vessels and proceeded to sea, no one knowing whither they went or hearing more of them' — Java's legend of a people swallowed by its own volcano.
summary.zh: 東爪哇瘟疫大作，少年王子離棄都城，西行另建新都——與此同時，克盧特山首次大爆發，聲如雷鳴，火山灰使舉國陷入『不可穿透之黑暗』。王子去後疫情不止，留居之人『乘舟出海，無人知其所往，亦再無音訊』——爪哇民族自述為自家火山所吞。

sensitivity.note: Catastrophe-migration legend around Kelud's first recorded eruption.

passages.text: The causes which induced him to leave his capital are related to have been a dreadful sickness, which at that period prevailed in the eastern districts of Java, and the designs of his minister. The first eruption of the mountain Kelud, of which tradition makes mention, is recorded to have taken place at this time, when the discharges from it are represented to have been like thunder, and the ashes to have involved the country in impenetrable darkness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles, History of Java (1817), vol. II ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sickness having continued to prevail after the departure of the prince, the inhabitants who had remained are said to have embarked in vessels and proceeded to sea, no one knowing whither they went or hearing more of them — the vanished fleet of the eastern kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Raffles (1817); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rice-Soul: Carrying the Rice-Child Home Under an Umbrella
title.zh: 稻之魂：以傘護送稻童歸家

region.en: Selangor rice-fields, Malay Peninsula (collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪稻田（斯凱特採錄）

texts.period: Ceremony recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), ch. V (vegetation charms)

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), the rice-soul ceremony (semangat padi)

summary.en: The rice has a soul, and the harvest is a rescue: the pawang leads a procession to the 'mother-sheaf', warning the herons and the 'spectral reapers' to retire; the cradle-basket of the Rice-child holds white cloth, parti-coloured thread, a hen's egg, a candle-nut, a cockle shell and a long iron nail; the first seven heads are cut into the cradle, rice is strewn over the sheaf and over the reapers' heads with 'kur semangat!' — 'cluck, cluck, soul!' — and the First Bearer slings the basket at her neck and opens an umbrella to shield the Rice-child from the sun on the road home.
summary.zh: 稻有魂，收穫即是救援：巫師（pawang）率隊至『母稻束』，先命蒼鷺與『幽靈收割者』退散；稻童之搖籃籃中置白布、五色線、雞蛋、蠟燭果、蛤殼與長鐵釘；先割七穗入籃，向母束與眾人頭上撒米，口中呼『庫·瑟瑪加！』——『咯咯，魂啊！』——首抬者以紅布將籃懸於頸間，撐傘遮陽，護『稻童』踏上歸家之路。

sensitivity.note: Rice-soul ceremony recorded 1900; paraphrase respectfully; the rice-mother theology parallels Dewi Sri across the archipelago.

passages.text: A shaped basket bound with the ribu-ribu creeper, standing in front of the three rice-baskets, was intended to serve as the cradle of the Rice-soul, or Rice-baby; it contained a strip of white cloth, parti-coloured thread, a hen's egg, a hard jungle-nut (candle-nut), a cockle shell, and a long iron nail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), the rice-soul ceremony; not verbatim.

passages.text: On reaching the rice the procession filed through a lane already made until the mother-sheaf was reached from which the Rice-soul was to be taken; the pawang warned the herons of the region to roost on his bow-shaft and bade the Spectral Reapers retire. The first seven heads were cut and deposited as before in the basket; rice was strewn over the sheaf, and tossed backwards over the reapers' heads, with the cry 'kur semangat, kur semangat!' — cluck, cluck, soul!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.

passages.text: The First Bearer slung the basket of the Rice-child about her neck and opened an umbrella to shield the Rice-child from the effects of the sun; without the umbrella, the recorders were told, the Rice-child could not be carried home — the harvest as a rescue of a soul small enough to sunburn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat (1900); not verbatim.

region.en: Selangor rivers, Malay Peninsula (collected by Skeat)
region.zh: 馬來半島雪蘭莪諸河（斯凱特採錄）

texts.period: Belief recorded 1890s; published Skeat, Malay Magic (1900)

source.work: W. W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), floods due to heavy rain (male and female floods)

summary.en: Floods, like other moving things, are conceived as male and female: floodwater 'due to heavy rain is conceived to be caused' by one sex of the water and the sudden spate that rolls down a river-bed by the other — the gendered taxonomy of the river's two tempers, recorded from the river-folk of Selangor.
summary.zh: 洪水如其他流動之物，亦有雌雄之分：驟雨之洪屬其一性，河道中奔突之暴漲屬另一性——雪蘭莪河民對河流兩副脾氣之性別分類。

sensitivity.note: River-lore record; read alongside the world-buffalo and tide-tree cosmologies.

passages.text: Floods, like other moving things, are conceived to be 'male' and 'female': the belief is that floods due to heavy rain are of one kind and the flood which sometimes rushes down a river-bed another — the river's two tempers given a gendered taxonomy in the Selangor river-lore collected by Skeat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Skeat, Malay Magic (1900); not verbatim.

title.en: Sri Tri Buana Buried on the Hill: The Offices of the New Court
title.zh: 三界之主葬於山丘：新朝廷之職官

texts.period: Composed as Sulalat al-Salatin c. 1612; Leyden translation 1821

source.work: Malay Annals, ch. IV (the death of Sri Tri Buana and the institution of the court offices), trans. John Leyden 1821

summary.en: When his earthly period was completed, Sri Tri Buana was buried on the hill of Singhapura; his son succeeds under a new title, and the court's constitution is fixed in the same breath as the mourning: the first bandahara Tun Parpatih Parmuka Barjaja, who occupies the sovereign's place when the sovereign will not show himself; the mantri opposite him; the pangulu bandahari; the chief hulubalang over all champions — the offices that will govern Malacca instituted at the founder's grave.
summary.zh: 斯里·三界之主壽終，葬於獅子城之丘；其子襲位並受新號；朝廷之憲制亦於此時同時確立：首位首相（bandahara）敦·帕帕提·帕爾穆卡·巴爾賈賈——王不露面時即代王位；其對座之大臣；彭古魯·邦達哈里；統領眾勇士之首席呼魯巴蘭——統治滿剌加之官制，即於開國者之墓前定立。

sensitivity.note: Court-constitution charter fixed at the founder's burial.

passages.text: After a long time, when his earthly period was completed, Sri Tri-buana departed this life, and was buried on the hill of Singhapura; he was succeeded by Raja Kichil Besar under the title of Paduca Sri Vicrama Vira. The constitution of the court was fixed with the mourning: Tun Parpatih Parmuka Barjaja became the first bandahara, and whenever the sovereign did not choose to show himself, his place was occupied by this minister; under him the pangulu bandahari, and the chief hulubalang who was over all the champions — the offices instituted at the founder's grave and carried on to Malacca.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Malay Annals ch. IV (Leyden 1821); not verbatim.
